patient_information: A 31-year-old woman from northern Tanzania, married with three children, with no significant past or family medical history. She does not smoke or take alcohol, and her HIV status was negative during her last pregnancy 12 months prior. There is no history of trauma.
chief_complaint: Loss of power and feeling in her legs for two days.
history_of_present_illness: The patient was well until two days prior to presentation when she experienced acute, severe, continuous, burning back pain that radiated in a band-like fashion to her umbilicus, unrelieved by analgesics or position. Within 12 hours, the pain lessened, but she developed ascending numbness in her feet and legs up to her waist, loss of leg power, and loss of bladder control. She had a febrile illness three weeks previously which was treated as malaria.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is from northern Tanzania. No other specific travel, vector, animal, or occupational exposures are mentioned.
vitals: Vital signs were normal upon clinical examination.
physical_exam: The patient was well-nourished with an unremarkable general examination, including no spinal tenderness, deformity, or gibbus. Neurologically, she was fully oriented with normal higher mental functions, cranial nerves, and upper limbs. Examination of the lower limbs revealed a flaccid paraparesis with a sensory level at T10. Her feet were in a slightly plantarflexed position. Tone was reduced, power was MRC grade 1/5 in all muscle groups, and reflexes were absent bilaterally. Plantar reflexes were extensor. Sensation to light touch was reduced up to the umbilicus, with impaired joint position sense in the feet and ankles and absent vibration sense up to the anterior iliac crests.
labs_and_diagnostics: Full blood count, renal, and liver function tests were normal. ESR was <10 mm/h. Serological tests for HIV (Serology and p24 Antigen), VDRL, and schistosomiasis were negative. Urine and stool analysis for Schistosoma ova were also negative. X-rays of the chest and thoracolumbar spine were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed a normal opening pressure, 11 white cells/μl (90% lymphocytes), and an elevated protein of 1.11 g/L. CSF glucose was normal, and Gram stain, Ziehl-Neelsen stain, Xpert MTB/RIF, and VDRL were all negative.
differential_diagnosis: The primary clinical syndrome was acute flaccid paraparesis. The differential diagnosis included lesions of the peripheral nerves (polyneuropathy) and acute spinal cord lesions (myelopathy). The presence of a distinct sensory level at T10 and extensor plantar reflexes localized the lesion to the spinal cord. For a non-compressive myelopathy, the main considerations were acute transverse myelitis and vascular spinal cord ischaemia (“spinal stroke”).
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was treated with corticosteroids and acyclovir. Management also included supportive care such as patient and family counselling, physiotherapy, regular turning, analgesia, and urinary catheterization. After three weeks of treatment, she showed partial improvement. At discharge, the power in her legs had improved to MRC grade 2-3/5, and she had a urinary catheter in situ. She was scheduled for outpatient follow-up.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is acute transverse myelitis. This is based on the acute onset of flaccid paraparesis with a distinct sensory level at T10 and bladder dysfunction, which localizes the lesion to the spinal cord. The diagnosis was confirmed by cerebrospinal fluid analysis showing inflammatory changes, specifically an increased lymphocyte count and elevated protein level. Extensive investigations ruled out common infectious causes in the region, including HIV, syphilis, tuberculosis, and schistosomiasis, making this a case of idiopathic acute transverse myelitis.
